column2: The date is set and the word goes out: there will be a feast in my hall. For the next fortnight the steward will haggle with butchers and vintners, the kitchens will not sleep, and every wandering performer for fifty leagues will come knocking at the gate.
Let it be a feast they remember.

A troupe of Strigany jugglers has pitched its painted wagons outside the walls. Their headman, all gold teeth and bows, offers to keep knives, torches and live ferrets in the air above my guests' heads every night of the feast, for a modest fee.
A wandering minstrel with a battered lute and a voice like honey asks for a place by the fire. He knows a hundred songs, he says, of old wars, lost loves and lords far greedier than me.
A band of musicians, pipers, a drummer and a hurdy-gurdy man, offers to play through the feast. They promise dances my guests will still be humming at the next harvest.
Travelling fire-eaters ask to perform. They breathe flame higher than the rafters, they say, and have only set fire to one hall, years ago, and that was the brewer's fault.

A conjurer in a moth-eaten robe sewn with stars offers to amaze my guests with vanishing coins, talking doves and a severed head that sings. He swears it is all sleight of hand and not a whisper of the Winds of Magic. The witch hunters seldom ask before they light the pyre.
A family of acrobats, the smallest no older than six, asks for a place. They tumble, they stand on each other's shoulders four high, and the father walks a rope stretched between the rafters.
A troupe of dancers in bright silks and bells asks to perform. They have danced, they say, before merchant princes in Tilea and a sultan in Araby, and have the stories to prove it.
Give them a place at the feast.
Send them on their way.
Hand the conjurer to the witch hunters.
Word spreads that you pay hedge wizards to perform under your roof.

The steward lays the kitchen accounts before me. Swans and peacocks, spiced wine from the south and a sugar subtlety in the shape of my castle, or honest beef and good bread, or something cheaper still. The guests will judge me by my table.

The brewmaster and the steward have argued for three days and come to me to settle it. A dwarf feast is judged by its ale before its meat: the old casks from the deep cellars, the good ale from the hold, or whatever is left in the barrels.

My cooks have not slept for a week. They argue over the menu, first breakfast through to the late supper, and come to me to settle it before someone is hit with a ladle. Every halfling at the table will judge me by the pies.
Spare nothing. Seven courses and a subtlety.
A good table, no more.
Bread and small beer will do.
We will cook from my book of recipes.
Let us make use of this little book.
You find yourself unable to put the book down...
Your [potential_cannibal.GetFirstName] takes charge of the kitchens, and of the book...

[feast_steward.GetTitledFirstName] reports that the beams over the great hall are rotten, the cellar floods every time it rains and the chimney in the kitchens has cracked. Something must be done before the guests arrive.
Mend it properly.
Hang tapestries over the worst of it.

A robber band has been working the road to my seat. Merchants have been stripped to their shirts and a tax collector was found hanging from an oak. My guests will ride that road. [feast_marshal.GetTitledFirstName] offers to take the garrison out and clear them.
Clear the road.
My guests have swords of their own.
[feast_marshal.GetTitledFirstName] proposes a boar hunt in the forest to fill the spits. The boars are fat this year, and vicious with it.
You go, [feast_marshal.GetFirstName].
Send one of my children.
I will ride out myself.
Mutton will do.
The kitchens are ready, the cellars are full and the hall is swept. The riders wait in the yard with the invitations in their saddlebags.
Ride!
Your vassals are invited. The guests who come will arrive in 20 days.
My liege, [From.GetTitledFirstName], invites me to a great feast in [From.GetHerHis] hall. There will be food, wine, performers and every other vassal of the realm.
I will ride to the feast.
Send my regrets.
[From.GetTitledFirstName] will hear that you are not coming.
[From.GetTitledFirstName] sends regrets. Pressing matters, a sick horse, a bad back. Whatever the reason, [From.GetSheHe] will not sit at my table.
I will remember this.
The guests have arrived. Their banners hang from the walls, their horses fill the stables and their servants fill the kitchens. Tonight the feast begins.
The day of the feast has come, and no one has. The tables are laid, the meat is turning on the spits, and the great hall is empty but for me and the dogs.
Let the feast begin!
Give the meat to the servants.
I have arrived at the hall of my liege, [From.GetTitledFirstName]. A servant shows me to my seat, a cup is filled before I sit, and the feast begins.
To our host!

The servants carry in roast swan dressed in its own feathers, a boar's head with an apple in its jaws, eels in jelly, spiced wine and a castle of sugar and almond. [From.GetTitledFirstName] has spared nothing.
Magnificent! I have never eaten so well.
Such waste, while the peasants starve.
Eat and say nothing.
[From.GetTitledFirstName] is pleased that you enjoyed the food.
[From.GetTitledFirstName] does not like hearing [From.GetHerHis] table mocked.
The table of [From.GetTitledFirstName] is an honest one: good beef, fresh bread, decent wine. Nothing that will be remembered, nothing to complain of.
A fine table.
Is this all?
Eat and say nothing.

Stale bread, a thin pottage, sour wine and a few pieces of grey mutton. Either [From.GetTitledFirstName] is poorer than [From.GetSheHe] lets on, or [From.GetSheHe] thinks very little of [From.GetHerHis] guests.
A sober table becomes a lord.
My hounds eat better than this.
Eat and say nothing.
[From.GetTitledFirstName] raises [From.GetHerHis] cup to my kitchens before the whole hall. My cooks will be unbearable for a month.
A guest with taste.
[From.GetTitledFirstName] made sure the whole hall heard what [From.GetSheHe] thinks of my food.
Ungrateful wretch.
The Strigany jugglers take the floor. Knives, torches and finally a very surprised ferret fly over the heads of my guests, and not one is dropped. The hall roars.
The minstrel sings of old wars and lost loves, and then a bawdy song about a lord very like one of my guests. By the last verse the whole hall is singing the chorus.
The musicians strike up, and soon the tables are pushed back and my guests are dancing, the old lords puffing and the young ones flushed and laughing.
The fire-eaters breathe flame up to the rafters, close enough to singe a beard or two. Only one tapestry catches fire, and it was an ugly one.
The conjurer pulls coins from ears, turns wine to water and back again and makes a dove vanish into thin air. The severed head that sings is a great success. No one asks where he got it.

The acrobats tumble down the length of the hall, stand four high on each other's shoulders, and the father walks the rope between the rafters with a cup of wine in each hand. He does not spill a drop.
The dancers whirl through the hall in silks and bells. The old lords forget their gout, the young ones forget their manners, and more than one guest's spouse forgets to look away.
What a night!
One of your guests will remember this show fondly.
The Strigany jugglers at the feast of [From.GetTitledFirstName] were the best I have ever seen.
I cannot get the minstrel's song out of my head. [From.GetTitledFirstName] knows how to entertain.
I danced until my feet bled at the feast of [From.GetTitledFirstName]. I have not been so happy in years.
The fire-eaters at the feast of [From.GetTitledFirstName] very nearly burned the hall down. It was magnificent.
The conjurer at the feast of [From.GetTitledFirstName] made my ring vanish and found it in my cup. I still do not know how he did it.
The acrobats at the feast of [From.GetTitledFirstName] walked the rafters like cats. I held my breath the whole time.
I will dream of the dancers at the feast of [From.GetTitledFirstName] for weeks.
A fine host.

Long after the hall has emptied, [feast_friend.GetTitledFirstName] and I are still sitting by the fire with the last jug of wine between us. We have talked of horses, wars, our children and our fathers, and found we agree on almost everything.
To friendship!
[feast_friend.GetTitledFirstName] becomes your friend.
It is late. Make my excuses and go to bed.
[From.GetTitledFirstName] and I talked until dawn at the feast. I think I have found a friend.
A good night.

In a dark corner of the hall I find [feast_friend.GetTitledFirstName], who likes our host no better than I do. Over a jug of wine we list everything [From.GetTitledFirstName] has done wrong. It is a long list, and a very pleasant evening.
We understand each other.
[feast_friend.GetTitledFirstName] becomes your friend.
Careless talk is dangerous. Go to bed.
[From.GetTitledFirstName] and I spent the feast agreeing about our liege. It is good to know I am not alone.
A friend in grievance.
The guests have gone to bed, but [feast_friend.GetTitledFirstName] lingers by the fire. We talk until the candles gutter, and it turns out we have more in common than fealty.
Pour another cup.
[feast_friend.GetTitledFirstName] becomes your friend.
A lord has no friends among his vassals.
My liege, [From.GetTitledFirstName], sat up with me half the night at the feast, and spoke to me as a friend.
I will not forget it.

[feast_duel_foe.GetTitledFirstName] has been needling me all evening, and now [feast_duel_foe.GetSheHe] says something about my mother that the whole table hears. My hand is on my sword before I know it.
Steel, then. In the yard, at dawn.
[feast_duel_foe.GetTitledFirstName] is challenged to a duel.
Not under my liege's roof.
[From.GetTitledFirstName] has thrown down a challenge before the whole hall. We are to fight in the yard at dawn.
I accept.
Your liege will not be pleased.
I will not fight.
My first cut opened [From.GetTitledFirstName] across the ribs, but [From.GetSheHe] is still on [From.GetHerHis] feet and coming at me.
My blow laid [From.GetTitledFirstName] open to the bone. [From.GetSheHe] will never be whole again, but [From.GetSheHe] is not done yet.
Have at you!
[From.GetTitledFirstName] strikes back.
Stay down!
My blade found [From.GetTitledFirstName], and the duel is over. [From.GetSheHe] will carry the wound for a while, and the memory longer.
My blade found [From.GetTitledFirstName], and the duel is over. [From.GetSheHe] will carry the mark of it until the day [From.GetSheHe] dies.
[From.GetTitledFirstName] lies dead in the trampled mud of the yard. The guests stand in silence, and then someone begins to clap.
First blood to me.
Your liege hears how the duel ended.
They will not forget me.
It is finished.
Two of my guests brawled in my yard at dawn and neither of them so much as scratched. My servants had to break it up before they started on each other with fists.
Fools, both of them.
[From.GetTitledFirstName] killed another guest in a duel in my yard this morning. The body has been laid out in the chapel, and the hall talks of nothing else.
A disgrace under my roof.
A fine display of steel.
[From.GetSheHe] will pay for the blood on my floor.
[From.GetTitledFirstName] wounded another guest in a duel in my yard this morning.
A disgrace under my roof.
A fine display of steel.
[From.GetSheHe] will pay for the blood on my floor.
[From.GetTitledFirstName] maimed another guest in a duel in my yard this morning. The surgeon says the arm will never be the same.
A disgrace under my roof.
A fine display of steel.
[From.GetSheHe] will pay for the blood on my floor.
Every time I set my cup down a servant fills it, and [From.GetTitledFirstName] is watching from the high table to see that I drink it.
Keep pace!
Cover the cup with my hand.
[From.GetTitledFirstName] is insulted.
[From.GetTitledFirstName] covered [From.GetHerHis] cup with [From.GetHerHis] hand when my servant came to fill it. In front of everyone.
Does my wine not suit?
I do not remember climbing onto the table. I do remember the song, and kicking the steward's accounts into the fire, and being carried out by four servants. So, I am told, does everyone else.
Was that me?
[From.GetTitledFirstName] is disgusted.
[From.GetTitledFirstName] climbed onto my high table to sing, kicked my steward's accounts into the fire and had to be carried out.
Disgusting.
I wake with my face in the gravy and a hall full of people laughing at me.
Was I snoring?
[From.GetTitledFirstName] is disgusted.
[From.GetTitledFirstName] fell asleep face down in the gravy at my high table and snored through the minstrel's best song.
Disgusting.

On the road to the feast my party was set upon by robbers. They took my purse, two of my horses and my good cloak, and I arrived at the gate of [From.GetTitledFirstName] in my shirt. What kind of lord lets brigands rule [From.GetHerHis] roads?
I will tell [From.GetHerHim] so.
[From.GetTitledFirstName] hears your complaint.
[From.GetTitledFirstName] was robbed on the road to my feast and arrived in [From.GetHerHis] shirt. [From.GetSheHe] wants to know what kind of lord lets brigands rule [From.GetHerHis] roads.
Make good the loss.
The roads are dangerous.
Send the marshal after them.
A clumsy serving boy has poured wine all down my sleeve. Before I have thought about it my knife is in his throat. He lies on the floor of the hall, and the music has stopped.
He should have been more careful.
[From.GetTitledFirstName] hears of it.
Pay his family before word gets out.

[From.GetTitledFirstName] has killed one of my serving boys in front of the whole hall, for spilling wine on [From.GetHerHis] sleeve. The boy's mother is screaming in the kitchens and the servants are watching to see what I will do.
Throw [From.GetHerHim] in the dungeon.
Pay the family from my own purse.
A servant is a servant.
For the life of one clumsy serving boy, [From.GetTitledFirstName] has thrown me in [From.GetHerHis] dungeon.
[From.GetSheHe] will regret this.
My jester has chosen tonight, before all my vassals, to make a jest of my rule. The hall laughs, and then the laughter dies as they look to see how I will take it.
To the dungeon with the fool!
Some of your guests think less of you for it.
Laugh along.
Your guests like a lord who can take a joke.
Answer the jest with a sharper one.
[From.GetTitledFirstName] threw the jester in the dungeon for a joke. A lord who cannot take a jest is a small lord.
Petty.
The jester mocked [From.GetTitledFirstName] to [From.GetHerHis] face before the whole hall, and [From.GetSheHe] took it in good humour.
A lord who can take a joke.

[feast_claim_holder.GetTitledFirstName] sits at my table, eating my food, drinking my wine and holding [feast_claim_title.GetName], which by rights should be mine. The doors are barred and my guards are at the walls.
Seize [feast_claim_holder.GetHerHim] at table.
Ask [feast_claim_holder.GetHerHim] for it.
[feast_claim_holder.GetTitledFirstName] decides.
Renounce my claim, in friendship.

Between courses, my liege [From.GetTitledFirstName] leans over and says, very pleasantly, that [feast_claim_title.GetName] should by rights be [From.GetHerHis], and that it would be a great kindness if I gave it up.
As my liege wishes.
[From.GetTitledFirstName] hears your answer.
I will not.
[From.GetTitledFirstName] hears your answer.
[From.GetTitledFirstName] has given me [feast_claim_title.GetName], as was only right.
A loyal vassal.
[From.GetTitledFirstName] has refused to give me [feast_claim_title.GetName].
I will not forget it.
[From.GetTitledFirstName] broke the oldest law there is and had me seized at [From.GetHerHis] own table. I am in [From.GetHerHis] dungeon, and the price of my freedom is [feast_claim_title.GetName].
I will rot first.
Take it and let me go.
[feast_flirt.GetTitledFirstName], spouse to another of the guests, has been catching my eye across the hall all evening, and smiling when I look back.
Remember my own vows.
Find a quiet corner.
[feast_flirt.GetTitledFirstName] decides.
[From.GetTitledFirstName] has slipped me a note: [From.GetSheHe] will be in the gallery above the hall after the music ends. My own spouse is deep in their cups.
Go to the gallery.
A child may come of this.
Go back to my spouse.
Word has come that [feast_affair_woman.GetTitledFirstName] is with child. I can count, and so, I fear, can [feast_affair_woman.GetHerHis] husband.
What is done is done.
[feast_lady.GetTitledFirstName] has smiled at me across the hall all evening, and laughed at my jokes a little longer than they deserved.
Not under my own roof.
Send a servant with a message.
[feast_lady.GetTitledFirstName] decides.
A servant of [From.GetTitledFirstName] has brought me a message: [From.GetSheHe] will be in [From.GetHerHis] chambers after the music ends, and the guards will not be at the door.
Go to [From.GetHerHim].
A child may come of this.
Stay with my own.
[From.GetTitledFirstName] is with child, and everyone at the feast saw where [From.GetSheHe] went after the music ended. [From.GetHerHis] husband most of all.
What is done is done.
[feast_daughter.GetTitledFirstName], daughter of [feast_daughter_parent.GetTitledFirstName], has been at my feast three nights, and I have not been able to look at anything else.
[feast_daughter.GetTitledFirstName], daughter of [feast_daughter_parent.GetTitledFirstName], has been at my father's feast three nights, and I have not been able to look at anything else.
Pay court to her.
[feast_daughter_parent.GetTitledFirstName] is flattered.
Take her to bed.
[feast_daughter_parent.GetTitledFirstName] finds out.
Keep my distance.
[From.GetTitledFirstName] has spent the feast paying court to my daughter, and the whole hall has seen it. Our family is going up in the world.
My daughter!
[From.GetTitledFirstName] has bedded my daughter under the roof where I am a guest. The whole hall knows it.
Protest before the whole hall.
Your liege hears you.
Say nothing, and remember.
Your liege knows what you think.
[From.GetTitledFirstName] stood up in my hall and called me a seducer of maidens before all my vassals, because of [From.GetHerHis] daughter.
[From.GetTitledFirstName] stood up in my hall and called my son a seducer of maidens before all my vassals, because of [From.GetHerHis] daughter.
How dare [From.GetSheHe]!
[From.GetTitledFirstName] said nothing about me and [From.GetHerHis] daughter, but [From.GetSheHe] has not met my eye since.
[From.GetTitledFirstName] said nothing about my son and [From.GetHerHis] daughter, but [From.GetSheHe] has not met my eye since.
Let [From.GetHerHim] sulk.
My daughter, [feast_daughter.GetFirstName], is with child, and the father is [feast_seducer.GetTitledFirstName]. I will not have my grandchild born a bastard.
[feast_seducer.GetFirstName] must marry her!
My liege must make [feast_seducer.GetFirstName] marry her!
[feast_seducer.GetTitledFirstName] is asked to marry [feast_daughter.GetFirstName].
[feast_love_host.GetTitledFirstName] is asked to order the wedding.
Hold my anger.
[From.GetTitledFirstName] has come to my hall and demands that I marry [From.GetHerHis] daughter, [feast_daughter.GetFirstName], who carries my child.
I will marry her.
I will not.
[From.GetTitledFirstName] has come to my hall and demands that my son [feast_seducer.GetFirstName] marry [From.GetHerHis] daughter, [feast_daughter.GetFirstName], who carries his child.
Order him to marry her.
[feast_seducer.GetFirstName] is ordered to marry.
My son can do better.
My father has ordered me to marry [feast_daughter.GetFirstName], who carries my child.
As my father commands.
I will not marry her.
The feast is over. My guests ride home with sore heads, full bellies and a good word for their host.
A feast to remember.
Your guests enjoyed the feast.
The feast at the hall of [From.GetTitledFirstName] is over, and I ride home with a sore head and a full belly.
What a feast.
War, or worse, has come, and there can be no feast now. The tables are cleared, the performers are paid off and my guests are sent home.
Another time.
Your guests are sent home.
My liege, [From.GetTitledFirstName], has cancelled the feast. The tables are cleared and the guests are sent home.
A pity.

[feast_rival_drinker.GetTitledFirstName] slams a tankard down before me and challenges me, before the whole hall, to match [feast_rival_drinker.GetHerHim] cup for cup until one of us is under the table.

[feast_rival_drinker.GetTitledFirstName] slams a tankard down before me and swears by [feast_rival_drinker.GetHerHis] beard that no one in this hall can drink a dwarf under the table. The whole hall turns to see what I will say.
Fill the tankards!
You are the last one standing.
You wake under the table.
I keep a clear head.
Have the cupbearer water my wine.
The trick is discovered.
